channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: [23] Cost-Effectiveness of Early Dose Reduction or Discontinuation Versus Antipsychotic Maintenance After First-Episode Psychosis: Results From the HAMLETT Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study assessed the cost-effectiveness of early antipsychotic dose reduction or discontinuation versus maintenance treatment in 347 remitted first-episode psychosis (FEP) patients over 24 months, using a trial-based cost-utility analysis alongside the HAMLETT RCT. The clinical question was whether reducing or stopping antipsychotics after remission is a cost-effective alternative to standard maintenance therapy.
FINDINGS: Early dose reduction/discontinuation led to lower QALYs (-0.077) and higher costs (€23,563) compared to maintenance over 24 months. The incremental net monetary benefit was -€27,430 at a €50,000/QALY threshold, with only ~9% probability of being cost-effective. A subgroup analysis suggested a small, uncertain benefit among female participants.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is robust due to the RCT design, societal perspective, and sensitivity analyses, but the 24-month horizon may be too short to capture long-term benefits (e.g., metabolic or functional gains). The negative cost-effectiveness result is consistent across scenarios, though subgroup findings warrant cautious exploration. The study’s funding sources are not reported, which is a minor limitation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For now, maintenance antipsychotic treatment after FEP remission remains the more cost-effective strategy. Clinicians should individualize decisions, particularly for female patients, but prioritize evidence-based maintenance unless clear benefits of reduction emerge over longer follow-up.

item.title: [17] HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY IN ALCOHOL-RELATED CIRRHOSIS:A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF CLINICAL CHARACTERISTICS, THERAPEUTIC STRATEGIES, AND PROGNOSTIC OUTCOMES.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PRISMA 2020) examined hepatic encephalopathy (HE) in alcohol-related cirrhosis (ARC), synthesizing evidence from 14 studies (n=6,185) to clarify clinical characteristics, treatments, and outcomes in this understudied subgroup.
FINDINGS: HE prevalence in ARC was 18.5% during hospitalization, with 90-day mortality at 12.1%. HE correlated with higher mortality (HR 3.1 at 90 days; HR 2.9 at 1 year), and active alcohol use worsened prognosis (HR 2.5). For secondary prophylaxis, rifaximin reduced recurrence (HR 0.42), often as adjunct to lactulose; lactulose alone also outperformed placebo. In acute HE, polyethylene glycol showed faster improvement than lactulose, though evidence was sparse.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is low-certainty (GRADE) due to heterogeneity, mixed-etiology cohorts, and observational designs with potential confounding. While associations between HE, mortality, and alcohol use are strong, causality cannot be inferred. The rifaximin and lactulose data are suggestive but rely on small, indirect studies. Polyethylene glycol’s benefit is preliminary and warrants further RCT validation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings support aggressive secondary prophylaxis (rifaximin + lactulose) in ARC-related HE, but definitive ARC-specific guidelines are lacking. Clinicians should prioritize alcohol abstinence and monitor HE recurrence closely; polyethylene glycol may be considered for acute HE pending stronger trials.

item.title: [15] Ketamine/Esketamine in Clinical Practice: Areas of Consensus and Nonconsensus from an American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology (ASCP) Delphi Panel Task Force.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology (ASCP) Delphi panel sought expert consensus on practical use of ketamine/esketamine for mood disorders in real-world settings, where evidence lags behind clinical implementation. The task force comprised 21 international academic psychiatrists with ketamine/esketamine expertise.
FINDINGS: Consensus (≥75% agreement) was reached on 35 of 105 items (33%), covering diagnostic indications, contraindications, dosing limits, racemic vs enantiomeric preparations, delivery routes, safety monitoring, access, and outcome criteria. Major areas of non-consensus included novel formulations (oral/IM), high-dose infusions, ketamine-assisted psychotherapy, and use beyond major depressive disorder.
INTERPRETATION: The low consensus rate (33%) highlights substantial uncertainty and gaps between real-world practice and the evidence base. Strengths include a structured Delphi process with predefined consensus thresholds and expert input; limitations include reliance on expert opinion rather than empirical data and potential selection bias among panel members. The findings underscore the need for targeted research to inform routine care decisions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current practice lacks robust evidence for many key decisions; clinicians should proceed cautiously, prioritize safety monitoring, and consider enrolling patients in studies to address uncertainties, especially regarding novel formulations and indications.

item.title: [15] Internet-based exercise interventions for the treatment of depression and anxiety: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 randomised controlled trials (RCTs) examined whether internet-based structured exercise interventions reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety compared with non-exercise controls in adults, addressing access barriers to conventional treatments.
FINDINGS: Across 11 RCTs (n=1,066), internet-based exercise produced a moderate reduction in depressive symptoms (standardised mean difference [SMD] −0.53, 95% CI −0.80 to −0.26; I²=77.2%). In 7 RCTs (n=607), a smaller but statistically significant reduction in anxiety symptoms was observed (SMD −0.41, 95% CI −0.65 to −0.17; I²=48.9%). Most trials had “some concerns” for risk of bias, and the certainty of evidence was rated low for depression and moderate for anxiety.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests internet-based exercise can modestly alleviate depressive and anxiety symptoms, but high heterogeneity for depression and risk-of-bias concerns limit confidence. The moderate-certainty finding for anxiety is more robust, yet effect sizes are small-to-moderate and may not translate to clinically meaningful changes for all patients. Long-term durability and implementation in routine care remain uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Internet-based exercise could serve as an adjunctive, low-risk option for patients unable or unwilling to engage in face-to-face therapy, but clinicians should set expectations about modest benefits and monitor symptom trajectories closely.

item.title: [14] Establishing the Clinical Role of Digital Therapeutics in Major Depressive Disorder Treatment: A Consensus Panel Perspective.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: A multidisciplinary expert consensus panel (May 2026) addressed how digital therapeutics (DTx) for major depressive disorder (MDD) should be evaluated, selected, and implemented in routine care across the US and Europe, given growing evidence of efficacy but low clinical adoption.
FINDINGS: The panel issued four consensus statements: DTx are a distinct treatment category to be judged primarily on efficacy; they can be used at multiple stepped-care stages (e.g., bridge-to-care, augmentation); clinician unfamiliarity, implementation hurdles, and engagement uncertainty are key barriers; and recommendations aim to guide clinician selection and integration of evidence-based DTx.
INTERPRETATION: This is a consensus document, not empirical research, so its strength lies in expert agreement rather than measured effect sizes or controlled comparisons. The statements align DTx with other evidence-based MDD treatments and outline practical pathways, but they do not quantify clinical outcomes or cost-effectiveness. External validity is limited by the US/European focus and the lack of patient/public representation in the panel.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The consensus provides a pragmatic framework for clinicians to consider DTx as part of stepped-care, but adoption should still be individualized and monitored for engagement and safety until higher-quality evidence accumulates.

item.title: [14] Clinical Course and Discontinuation of Olanzapine Long-Acting Injectable: A Retrospective Case Series Including a Case of Post-Injection Delirium/Sedation Syndrome.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective case series examined real-world discontinuation rates and reasons for stopping olanzapine long-acting injectable (OLAI) in 30 outpatients with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders across three behavioral health clinics, focusing on barriers such as post-injection delirium/sedation syndrome (PDSS) and monitoring burden.
FINDINGS: OLAI was discontinued in 19 patients (63.3%). Reasons included refusal/nonadherence (n=7), perceived lack of efficacy (n=5), adverse effects (n=4), transfer of care (n=3), monitoring burden (n=3), operational barriers (n=2), medication shortage (n=1), and PDSS (n=1). PDSS occurred after extended OLAI tolerability and required emergency evaluation with several days of delirium.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides descriptive real-world data but is limited by its small, retrospective, uncontrolled design and lack of standardized outcome assessment. The high discontinuation rate (63.3%) and heterogeneous reasons suggest practical and tolerability challenges, particularly the 3-hour post-injection monitoring burden. PDSS, though rare, had severe consequences. The evidence is preliminary and does not support causal inferences about risk factors or predictors of discontinuation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should anticipate high discontinuation rates with OLAI due to nonadherence, perceived inefficacy, and logistical barriers. PDSS, though uncommon, is a serious risk requiring emergency preparedness. These findings support careful patient selection, shared decision-making, and local protocol optimization rather than broad changes in practice based on risk-factor inference.

item.title: [13] Mobile Units for Integrated Addiction and HIV Prevention Services for People Who Inject Drugs: The HPTN 094 Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This open-label randomized clinical trial (HPTN 094) tested whether mobile units delivering integrated HIV preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) and medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) with peer navigation improved PrEP and MOUD use compared with peer navigation alone in people who inject drugs (PWID) across five U.S. cities.
FINDINGS: At 26 weeks, confirmed PrEP use was 5.4% (11/203) in the intervention arm vs 2.9% (6/206) in controls (p-value not reported), and MOUD use was 14.8% (30/203) vs 10.7% (22/206). At 52 weeks, PrEP use was 2.0% (4/203) vs 1.9% (4/206) and MOUD use was 13.3% (27/203) vs 14.1% (29/206). HIV incidence was low (0.9 per 100 person-years; 95% CI 0.2–2.6), with 1 vs 2 acquisitions. All-cause mortality was lower in the intervention arm (4 vs 13 deaths; hazard ratio 0.29; 95% CI 0.1–0.9; P = .03).
INTERPRETATION: The trial shows no meaningful improvement in PrEP or MOUD uptake from mobile integrated services versus peer navigation alone, despite a mortality signal favoring the intervention. The mortality finding is intriguing but should be interpreted cautiously due to the open-label design, small event count, and lack of adjustment for multiple comparisons. The low PrEP uptake in both arms highlights persistent barriers to prevention engagement among PWID.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Mobile integrated services did not outperform peer navigation for primary outcomes, so current practice should prioritize accessible peer navigation and harm reduction services. The mortality reduction merits further investigation but is not yet sufficient to change policy or practice.

item.title: [12] One-year efficacy of the LIFESTYLE intervention in improving diet, physical activity and reducing alcohol use in overweight people with severe mental illness: multicentre randomised controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: People with severe mental illness (SMI) have high rates of unhealthy diet, physical inactivity and alcohol use, contributing to premature mortality. This multicentre RCT from six Italian universities tested whether the structured LIFESTYLE psychoeducational programme improves diet, physical activity and reduces alcohol use versus a less structured psychoeducational comparator in 401 adults with SMI over 1 year.
FINDINGS: At 1-year follow-up, the intervention increased odds of higher weekly METs for total activity (OR 1.43, 95% CI 1.08–1.89; p<0.01), walking (OR 1.50, 95% CI 1.18–1.90; p<0.001) and moderate activity (OR 1.85, 95% CI 1.24–2.77; p<0.01). Dietary improvements included higher intake of fish (OR 1.67, 95% CI 1.45–1.97; p<0.05), fresh fruit (OR 1.36, 95% CI 1.05–1.76; p<0.05) and vegetables (OR 1.91, 95% CI 1.56–1.96; p<0.05), reduced junk food (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.63–0.99; p<0.05) and lower daily alcohol use (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.52–0.95; p<0.05).
INTERPRETATION: The trial shows moderate but statistically significant improvements in lifestyle metrics at 1 year, with effect sizes modest (ORs mostly 1.3–1.9). The multicentre design and use of GEE strengthen internal validity, but blinding was not possible and the comparator was an active psychoeducational programme, limiting the ability to attribute effects solely to the LIFESTYLE structure. Long-term clinical outcomes (e.g., cardiovascular events, BMI, mortality) were not assessed, so clinical significance remains uncertain. External validity may be limited to Italian SMI populations receiving structured psychoeducation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The LIFESTYLE programme may be a useful adjunct to routine care for improving diet, activity and alcohol use in SMI, but the modest effect sizes and lack of hard clinical endpoints suggest it should be implemented alongside, rather than as a replacement for, standard lifestyle interventions. Monitor adherence and sustainability of changes in real-world settings.

item.title: [11] From Toad Venom to Drug Development: The Clinical Pharmacology of Mebufotenin (5-MeO-DMT) in Treatment-Resistant Depression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the clinical pharmacology of mebufotenin (5-MeO-DMT) as a potential treatment for treatment-resistant depression (TRD), summarising receptor binding, metabolism, and early clinical efficacy data from a single phase 2b trial.
FINDINGS: Mebufotenin shows high affinity for 5-HT1A (Ki 3.0 nM) and 30–300-fold lower affinity for 5-HT2A, with clearance via monoamine oxidase A. In the phase 2b trial (GH001-TRD-201), inhaled GH001 produced a placebo-adjusted MADRS reduction of −15.5 points at day 8 (p < 0.001; d = −2.0), with 57.5% (23/40) achieving remission versus 0% (0/41) on placebo. Among remitters, 87.0% (20/23) remained in remission at 6 months with as-needed retreatment. Psychoactive effects lasted 9–14 minutes, and 97.5% of patients were discharge-ready within 1 hour. No serious treatment-related adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and rests on a single small phase 2b trial without protocol-mandated psychotherapy, limiting generalisability and raising questions about expectancy effects and the role of psychological support. The large effect size (d = −2.0) and high remission rate are striking but require replication in larger, adequately blinded phase 3 trials with diverse populations to confirm efficacy, durability, and safety. The short duration of action and lack of serious adverse events are notable, but long-term risks remain uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data suggest potential rapid antidepressant effects of inhaled 5-MeO-DMT in TRD, but routine use cannot be recommended until robust phase 3 evidence is available. Clinicians should await larger trials before considering this intervention outside research settings.

item.title: [10] Comparative Effectiveness of Haloperidol, Droperidol, and Ondansetron for Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome in the Emergency Department.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This multicenter retrospective cohort study (2014–2024) compared haloperidol, droperidol, and ondansetron for adults with suspected cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) in the ED, focusing on short-term ED recidivism and secondary outcomes such as hospital admission and adverse events.
FINDINGS: After propensity-score matching, 72-hour ED recidivism was lower with haloperidol vs. ondansetron (8.2% vs. 15.1%; OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.41–0.62; p < 0.0001) and with droperidol vs. ondansetron (7.4% vs. 14.0%; OR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32–0.76; p = 0.0014). No significant difference was found between droperidol and haloperidol (7.5% vs. 9.8%; OR 0.75, 95% CI 0.47–1.20; p = 0.23). Multivariable Cox models confirmed lower return risk with haloperidol (HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.49–0.79) and droperidol (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.56–0.83). Adverse events were rare across groups.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides moderate-strength observational evidence that haloperidol and droperidol reduce short-term ED recidivism compared with ondansetron in suspected CHS. Key limitations include retrospective design, reliance on ICD-10 coding, potential unmeasured confounding (e.g., cannabis use patterns, symptom severity), and lack of standardized dosing or follow-up. The effect sizes are modest and statistically robust but not necessarily clinically dramatic; adverse events were infrequently coded, which may underestimate true risk. Prospective randomized trials are needed to confirm efficacy, optimal dosing, and safety.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest haloperidol or droperidol may be reasonable alternatives to ondansetron for acute symptom control in suspected CHS, particularly in patients with recurrent ED visits. However, due to study limitations, routine practice change should await confirmatory trials; clinicians should monitor for extrapyramidal symptoms and QT prolongation when using antipsychotics in this context.

item.title: [9] Changes in the profile of adults diagnosed as autistic since 2010: population-based studies in the UK and Sweden.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This population-based cohort study from the UK and Sweden examined trends in adult autism diagnoses since 2010, focusing on sociodemographic shifts and co-occurring neuropsychiatric conditions. It used primary care records (UK, 2010–2023) and national registers (Sweden, 2010–2021) to assess incidence, prevalence, and prior mental health histories among adults diagnosed with autism.
FINDINGS: The study included 24.5 million adults in the UK (141,119 with autism) and 9.1 million in Sweden (100,817 with autism). Incident adult autism diagnoses rose fastest in 16–20-year-olds and females in both countries, with white ethnic groups in the UK and individuals with Swedish-born parents in Sweden showing the steepest increases. Over time, prior diagnoses of epilepsy, psychosis, and intellectual disability declined among newly diagnosed autistic adults, while histories of ADHD, anxiety, and depression increased markedly. For example, in the UK, prior epilepsy among new autism diagnoses fell from 10% (95% CI 7.6–13%) in 2010 to 4% (95% CI 3.6–4.5%) in 2023, while prior anxiety rose from 28.7% (95% CI 24.4–33.6%) to 58.3% (95% CI 56.6–60.1%).
INTERPRETATION: The findings reflect substantial changes in who receives an autism diagnosis, with growing recognition among females and younger adults, and a shift toward higher psychiatric comorbidity. The study’s large, population-based design strengthens internal validity, though reliance on routine records may undercount undiagnosed or subthreshold cases. The decline in co-occurring intellectual disability and epilepsy suggests broadening diagnostic criteria or improved access, rather than true prevalence changes. External validity is high for both countries, but generalisability to other healthcare systems may be limited. The magnitude of change in psychiatric comorbidities is clinically meaningful and underscores the need for integrated mental health services for autistic adults.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should anticipate a more diverse autism population, with increasing psychiatric comorbidity, particularly anxiety and depression. Services must adapt to address these needs, while remaining cautious about potential overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis in groups with shifting sociodemographic profiles. Further research is needed to clarify whether these trends reflect improved recognition or diagnostic drift.

item.title: [9] Efficacy of Lumateperone 42 mg in Major Depressive Disorder: Subgroup Analysis of a Phase 3 Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This post hoc subgroup analysis of a phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT (Study 501) assessed whether adjunctive lumateperone 42 mg improves depressive symptoms in adults with DSM-5 major depressive disorder (MDD) and inadequate response to 1–2 antidepressant trials, across demographic and clinical subgroups.
FINDINGS: In the modified intent-to-treat population (n=481; lumateperone+ADT n=239, placebo+ADT n=242), lumateperone+ADT significantly improved MADRS Total score (LSMD −4.9, P<.0001), CGI-S score (LSMD −0.7, P<.0001), and QIDS-SR-16 score (LSMD −2.4, P<.0001) at Day 43. Significant MADRS improvements (P<.01) were observed across all demographic subgroups and baseline severity strata, with additional significant CGI-S and QIDS-SR-16 improvements (P<.05) in most subgroups.
INTERPRETATION: The study shows consistent statistical superiority of lumateperone+ADT over placebo+ADT across predefined subgroups, suggesting robustness of the overall trial result. However, as a post hoc analysis, it cannot establish causality for subgroup effects and carries a high risk of type I error inflation from multiple comparisons. The effect sizes (e.g., MADRS LSMD −4.9) are modest and of uncertain clinical significance in routine MDD care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support potential adjunctive use of lumateperone 42 mg in treatment-resistant MDD, but confirmation in prospective trials and evaluation of long-term safety and tolerability are needed before changing practice.

item.title: [8] Bridging Nonconsecutive Esketamine Weeks with Bupropion and Over-the-Counter Dextromethorphan.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: A single-patient case report describes whether over-the-counter dextromethorphan (DXM) plus bupropion XL can “bridge” non-consecutive weeks of intranasal esketamine maintenance in a 52-year-old woman with treatment-resistant depression and bipolar II disorder.
FINDINGS: Weekly esketamine reduced her PHQ-9 from 27 to 4 (±1). Delaying a dose by >10 days raised the PHQ-9 by ~8 points (4→12). Adding DXM 45 mg BID and continuing bupropion XL 450 mg daily allowed bi-weekly esketamine without relapse; she has remained stable for an unstated follow-up period.
INTERPRETATION: This is a single-case, open-label, uncontrolled N-of-1 report with no blinding, randomisation or comparator arm. The observed PHQ-9 shifts are large but based on one individual; causality, generalisability and long-term safety are unknown. The proposed NMDA-receptor mechanism is plausible but unproven in this context.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The regimen may be worth trialling in similar patients who cannot attend weekly visits, but only after discussing the lack of evidence, off-label status of OTC DXM, and potential drug–drug interactions with CYP2D6 inhibition.

item.title: [7] Awareness and Inclusion of Neurodiversity in the Healthcare Systems of Five Arab Countries: A Scoping Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review examined how five Arab countries (Saudi Arabia, Qatar, UAE, Oman, Jordan) address neurodiversity (including ASD, ADHD, intellectual disability, learning disorders) within their healthcare systems, using PRISMA-ScR methods to map policy progress, service access, and awareness gaps.
FINDINGS: Thirty-two studies were included, mostly published 2019–2025. Formal policies were largely autism-specific; Qatar’s National Autism Plan (2017) and Saudi Arabia’s national autism program were the most developed. Post-diagnostic intervention uptake was ~5% in Qatar’s screening program. Provider knowledge was low to moderate (competency scores below threshold in Saudi Arabia; primary-care gaps in Oman and Jordan). Access barriers included diagnostic delays (44.1% in Saudi Arabia), long waits for first intervention (up to 1 year in Qatar), cost (58% in Jordan), and lack of standardized guidelines, registries, and transition services. Telehealth reduced waiting times in the UAE (from 7.1 to 1.3 weeks).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited, heterogeneous, and largely descriptive, with no RCTs or meta-analyses. Strengths include systematic searching and dual screening, but reliance on observational and grey literature limits causal inference. Policy development is uneven, workforce capacity is weak, and service gaps are substantial. The clinical significance of findings is high given the documented disparities, but the lack of standardized outcomes and long-term follow-up constrains generalizability. More rigorous, interventional research is needed to assess the impact of policy changes and service models.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should anticipate delayed diagnoses, limited access to interventions, and low provider competence in neurodiversity care across these countries. Telehealth may offer practical solutions to reduce wait times, but systemic reforms in policy, training, and service integration are urgently required.

item.title: [7] [Opioid Misuse and New Prescribing Guidelines].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a narrative review from France describing trends in prescription opioid misuse (notably tramadol and codeine), the national addictovigilance surveillance system, and updated national prescribing guidelines aimed at safer opioid use while maintaining patient access.
FINDINGS: The article reports that France has not experienced an opioid crisis on the scale seen in North America, but signals of dependence and misuse have been detected, prompting regulatory responses. It highlights the role of the addictovigilance network in early detection and the integration of dependence risk assessment into routine prescribing. Key strategies include wider naloxone distribution, patient involvement in treatment decisions, and efforts to reduce stigma around dependence.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review without original data, this article provides an overview of surveillance and policy responses rather than quantitative evidence. Its strength lies in contextualizing opioid safety within a national framework, but it lacks effect sizes, comparative data, or rigorous study design. The recommendations are largely policy-driven and not directly tested in controlled trials. The clinical implications are framed at a system level rather than individual patient care.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This review does not change bedside practice through new clinical evidence but underscores the importance of routine screening for opioid dependence and harm reduction measures (e.g., naloxone availability) in France. Clinicians should remain alert to dependence risk with tramadol and codeine and integrate screening into prescribing workflows.

item.title: [7] RELAX Perinatal Digital Intervention to Prevent Increasing Anxiety: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The RELAX trial was a phase 2b, 2-arm, parallel-group, superiority randomized clinical trial (RCT) conducted in the UK from June 2023 to April 2025. It evaluated whether a pregnancy-tailored, self-led digital cognitive bias modification for interpretation (RELAX) added to usual maternity care (UC) could prevent increased anxiety during pregnancy and reduce anxiety, depression, repetitive negative thinking (RNT), and improve functioning compared with UC alone in pregnant individuals (16–28 weeks’ gestation) with high RNT and up to moderate anxiety.
FINDINGS: 268 participants were randomized (mean age 33.7 years; 64.9% married). At 8 weeks (T2), anxiety (GAD-7) was significantly lower in the RELAX group vs UC (mean difference −1.5; 95% CI −2.4 to −0.6; P = .001). Secondary outcomes at T2 also favored RELAX: depression (PHQ-9: −0.8; 95% CI −1.5 to −0.1), postnatal depression (EPDS: −1.1; 95% CI −2.0 to −0.2), RNT (RTQ-10: −2.7; 95% CI −4.5 to −0.9), worry (PSWQ: −3.6; 95% CI −5.9 to −1.3), and perinatal anxiety (PASS: −5.5; 95% CI −8.2 to −2.8). At 36 weeks (T3, 12–24 weeks postpartum), sustained effects were seen for general anxiety (GAD-7: −1.0; 95% CI −1.9 to −0.1), postnatal depression (EPDS: −1.3; 95% CI −2.4 to −0.2), and RNT (RTQ-10: −2.4; 95% CI −4.6 to −0.2). No significant differences were found in functioning (WSAS) or several secondary outcomes at T3. Mechanism analysis suggested improved interpretation bias did not mediate anxiety reduction.
INTERPRETATION: The trial shows a modest but statistically significant reduction in anxiety and related symptoms with the RELAX intervention compared with UC during pregnancy and early postpartum. Strengths include a rigorous RCT design, low attrition, and prespecified outcomes. However, effect sizes are small (e.g., GAD-7 difference of 1.5 points), and clinical significance is uncertain. The lack of mediation by interpretation bias and no clear functional benefit limit mechanistic and practical conclusions. Longer-term follow-up and replication in broader populations are needed.
