item.title: [6] Piloting New Medications for Borderline Personality Disorder: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in Psychopharmacological Research.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) currently lacks approved pharmacological treatments despite significant symptom burden. This in silico study pilots an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled framework to design a hypothetical novel compound (BPD-AI-01) targeting multiple therapeutic goals for BPD, using deep learning, natural language processing, and predictive modelling.
FINDINGS: The AI models generated BPD-AI-01, a candidate molecule predicted to act as a partial 5-HT1A agonist, NMDA modulator, and weak 5-HT2A/D2 antagonist, with low affinity for histaminergic and muscarinic receptors. Simulated symptom trajectories suggested potential antidepressant, anti-suicidal, mood-stabilising, and antipsychotic-like effects without marked sedation or weight gain. All analyses were based on publicly available data and in silico simulations; no empirical testing was conducted.
INTERPRETATION: This is a purely computational, hypothesis-generating study with no patient involvement or empirical validation. While the AI framework demonstrates feasibility for drug design, the findings are entirely theoretical and subject to the limitations of in silico predictions, including unvalidated algorithms, lack of real-world clinical data, and potential biases in training datasets. The clinical relevance remains entirely speculative until tested in controlled trials.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No immediate change to clinical practice is warranted. This study highlights a potential future direction for psychopharmacology in BPD but underscores the need for rigorous empirical validation before any consideration of clinical use.

item.title: [24] Clinical practice guideline recommendations for subthreshold depression in adults: A systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review synthesizes recommendations from clinical practice guidelines on the management of subthreshold depression (SD) in adults, a condition linked to increased risk of major depressive disorder (MDD) and other adverse outcomes. The study evaluates consistency across guidelines and compares recommendations for SD with those for mild MDD to contextualize treatment patterns.
FINDINGS: Thirteen guidelines were included, with most grouping SD alongside mild or mild-to-moderate MDD rather than addressing it separately. No guideline recommended routine antidepressant use for SD; when considered, antidepressants were reserved for specific circumstances. All guidelines with formal recommendations prioritized low-intensity psychosocial or psychological interventions or supportive care as initial management. For mild MDD, most guidelines aligned with this pattern, though a minority recommended antidepressants as standard options or more intensive psychotherapy requiring trained professionals.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is derived from guideline-level assessments rather than primary trials, limiting direct clinical inference but providing a coherent cross-guideline consensus. The methodological quality of included guidelines varied, and recommendations for SD were often embedded within broader depression categories, which may reduce specificity. The consistency in favoring low-intensity interventions over antidepressants for SD strengthens confidence in this pattern, though the lack of high-quality, SD-specific trials remains a gap. The findings are likely generalizable to routine psychiatric care settings where stepped-care principles are applied.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should prioritize low-intensity psychosocial or psychological interventions for subthreshold depression, reserving antidepressants for specific cases. The findings support a stepped-care approach, but the absence of SD-specific high-quality trials means further research is needed to refine recommendations.

item.title: [14] Cognitive Behavioral Therapy-Based Digital Interventions for Illicit Substance Use Disorders: Scoping Review of Intervention Design, Efficacy Indicators, and Methodological Gaps.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review mapped the design and delivery of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)-based digital interventions for illicit substance use disorders (SUDs), addressing gaps in access to conventional treatment and the underrepresentation of illicit substances in research. It synthesized empirical studies across platforms, frameworks, and outcomes using JBI scoping review methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting.
FINDINGS: Fifty-six studies (2008–2026) from 47 samples were included; 71.4% were from North America and 69.6% used randomized designs. Polysubstance use was most common (57.1%), followed by cannabis (23.2%), opioids (10.7%), and stimulants (8.9%). Interventions were mainly web- (42.9%) or app-based (42.9%), grounded in CBT (87.5%), often combined with contingency management (32.1%) or motivational interviewing (30.4%). Core components included therapeutic intervention (98.2%), self-tracking/notification (44.6%), rewards (42.9%), and support/feedback (37.5%). Primary outcomes focused on substance use/abstinence (73.2%), retention/feasibility (28.6%), and mental health/coping (25%). Reported limitations were predominantly participant-level (92.9%), measurement-level (76.8%), study-level (60.7%), and intervention-level (44.6%).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is heterogeneous, with varied populations, platforms, and methodological rigor. Most studies are small, short-term RCTs or pilot trials, limiting generalizability. Author-reported limitations highlight risks of bias, reliance on self-report, and lack of objective outcome measures. While digital CBT interventions show promise as adjuncts, their standalone efficacy remains unproven. Substance-specific trials with objective measures (e.g., toxicology) and longer follow-up are needed to establish clinical utility.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current CBT-based digital interventions may complement standard addiction care but should not replace it. Clinicians should use these tools cautiously, prioritizing evidence-based care and monitoring for engagement and outcomes. Future integration depends on stronger, more rigorous trials demonstrating meaningful, sustained benefits.

item.title: [14] Risk of cardiovascular events and mortality associated with LDL and non-HDL cholesterol levels after statin initiation for primary prevention: A multiregional cohort study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This multiregional cohort study (Hong Kong, New Zealand, UK) examined whether achieving lower LDL and non-HDL cholesterol levels after initiating statins for primary prevention reduces major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) or all-cause mortality, addressing uncertainty about guideline-recommended cholesterol targets.
FINDINGS: Among 185,237 statin initiators followed for a mean 5.4–6.5 years, multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) for MACE versus LDL ≥2.6 mmol/L were 0.80 (95% CI 0.77–0.83) for 1.8–2.5 mmol/L, 0.79 (0.66–0.94) for 1.4–1.7 mmol/L, and 0.82 (0.60–1.12) for <1.4 mmol/L. Non-HDL cholesterol showed similar graded reductions. Very low LDL (<1.4 mmol/L) and non-HDL (<2.6 mmol/L) were not associated with increased all-cause mortality (HRs ~1.0). Heterogeneity was noted, especially at lowest concentrations in New Zealand.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides moderate-strength evidence that lower achieved LDL/non-HDL after statin initiation is associated with reduced MACE, with no clear excess mortality at very low levels after adjustment. Strengths include large sample size and multi-country data; limitations include residual confounding, selection bias from landmark analysis, and heterogeneity across regions, particularly at extreme cholesterol levels.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For primary prevention patients on statins, aiming for guideline-recommended non-HDL <3.4 mmol/L (and likely LDL <1.8 mmol/L) appears reasonable to reduce cardiovascular events, without clear safety concerns at very low levels in adjusted analyses.

item.title: [10] Temporal cortical gray matter volume relates to symptom improvement during cognitive behavioral therapy for depression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This observational cohort study examined whether baseline cortical gray matter volume (GMV) predicts symptom improvement during six months of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) in 52 adults with unipolar depression versus 42 healthy controls, using structural MRI and multiple regression with FDR correction.
FINDINGS: Patients had higher baseline depressive symptoms and greater symptom reduction over six months than controls (both p < 0.001). In patients, larger right middle temporal gyrus (MTG) volume at baseline predicted greater symptom reduction (β = 0.55, pFDR = 0.033), explaining an additional 15% of variance beyond clinical variables; group GMV differences were not significant after FDR correction.
INTERPRETATION: The association between right MTG volume and CBT response is statistically robust after FDR correction but derives from a modest sample, lacks a non-therapy comparator, and cannot establish causality; effect sizes and confidence intervals are not reported, limiting clinical inference. Replication in larger, randomized cohorts with longer follow-up and active comparators is needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is insufficient to guide treatment selection or prognosis based on MTG volume; any bedside implication remains speculative until validated in routine care settings.

item.title: [9] Implementation of WHO Self-Help Plus among Ukrainian university students during wartime: A multicenter longitudinal study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: During active war in Ukraine, Ukrainian university students face high psychological distress. This multicenter longitudinal study tested whether the WHO Self-Help Plus (SH+), a brief Acceptance and Commitment Therapy-based program delivered by non-specialists, reduces distress and improves functioning in this setting.
FINDINGS: Of 297 students who completed the 5-week SH+ course, perceived stress, depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and post-traumatic stress (PCL-5) all decreased significantly from baseline to post-intervention; well-being (WHO-5) and daily functioning (WHODAS 2.0) improved and were maintained at 3-month follow-up. Resilience (CD-RISC-10) did not change. Implementation barriers included security threats, power outages, and academic scheduling conflicts, contributing to attrition.
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests SH+ can reduce distress and improve functioning in war-exposed students when delivered by trained non-specialists, with benefits sustained for three months. Strengths include a pragmatic, real-world setting and use of validated scales; limitations include lack of a control group, non-randomised design, and attrition not fully accounted for in analyses. Effect sizes and confidence intervals are not reported, so the magnitude of benefit remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SH+ may be a feasible first-line, low-intensity intervention for distressed university students in conflict zones, but confirmation in a randomised controlled trial is needed before widespread adoption.

item.title: [9] Targeted Use of Kudzu for Binge Drinking Among Adults With Alcohol Use Disorder: A Phase 2b Randomized Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b RCT (n=120) tested whether targeted as-needed kudzu extract (2 g on anticipated binge days) reduces binge drinking in adults with alcohol use disorder (AUD) receiving weekly counseling over 12 weeks.
FINDINGS: In intention-to-treat analysis, kudzu reduced binge-drinking days (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0.73, 95 % CI 0.54–0.99). In the as-treated cohort (≥2.7 days/week use), the effect was larger (IRR 0.58, 95 % CI 0.38–0.89). Secondary outcomes showed fewer binge weeks (RR 0.79, 95 % CI 0.62–0.99 ITT; RR 0.68, 95 % CI 0.47–0.98 as-treated) and lower PEth positivity (RR 0.82, 95 % CI 0.67–0.99). Benefits persisted at 3-month follow-up (RR 0.68, 95 % CI 0.47–0.97). Adverse events were similar between groups; no serious kudzu-related events occurred.
INTERPRETATION: The trial suggests a modest but statistically significant reduction in binge-drinking days with targeted kudzu, particularly among adherent participants. Strengths include double-blinding, high retention (88 %), and objective biomarker corroboration. Limitations include reliance on self-reported drinking, modest sample size, and absence of a standard-of-care comparator (e.g., naltrexone). Effect sizes are small-to-moderate; clinical significance remains uncertain until replicated in larger trials with longer follow-up and broader outcome measures.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is insufficient to recommend kudzu as routine AUD pharmacotherapy. It may be considered as an adjunct for patients motivated to reduce binge episodes, with careful monitoring for adherence and tolerability.

item.title: [9] Deficient Monetary Reward Processing in Schizophrenia: A Meta-Analysis and Computational Modeling of a Monetary Incentive Delay Task.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This meta-analysis and computational modeling study examined monetary reward processing deficits in schizophrenia (SZ) using the Monetary Incentive Delay (MID) task, comparing 785 SZ patients with 755 healthy controls (HCs) across 30 studies, plus an independent subject-level analysis of 60 SZ and 74 HC participants.
FINDINGS: The meta-analysis found small-to-moderate behavioral differences in SZ, including prolonged reaction times (RT) and reduced correct response rates (CR) on reward trials. In the subject-level study, SZ patients showed prolonged RT, lower CR on reward and loss trials, and higher CR on neutral trials, alongside higher absolute reward prediction error (PE) and absolute loss PE, lower reward expected-value (Q), and more negative loss-Q. Loss-related indices (ABSLPE, Loss-Q) correlated with negative symptom severity (PANSS-N).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests consistent but modest deficits in reward processing in SZ, supported by both behavioral and computational modeling data. Strengths include a large meta-analytic sample and independent validation. However, the clinical significance of these computational indices remains uncertain, as effect sizes are small and longitudinal validation is lacking. The Rescorla-Wagner model used may not capture all aspects of reward learning, and associations with symptoms are correlational.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings highlight potential biomarkers for motivational deficits in SZ but do not yet translate to routine practice. Further research is needed to determine if these indices predict treatment response or functional outcomes.

item.title: [9] [Xanomeline-trospium: A review of clinical studies in patients with schizophrenia].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Xanomeline-trospium (KarXT), a muscarinic M1/M4 agonist with a novel antipsychotic mechanism, was approved in the US in 2024 for schizophrenia. This systematic review synthesises randomised controlled trials (RCTs) on its efficacy and tolerability in adults with schizophrenia.
FINDINGS: Three placebo-controlled phase 2/3 RCTs (n = 690) showed statistically significant and clinically relevant reductions in total PANSS scores with xanomeline-trospium versus placebo (differences −8 to −12 points). Adverse events were mainly transient peripheral cholinergic effects; rates of sedation, extrapyramidal symptoms, weight gain and prolactin elevation were similar to placebo. Evidence for negative and cognitive symptom improvement was inconclusive.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate in size and of high internal validity (RCTs, registered trials), but external validity is limited by short-term follow-up and lack of active-comparator data. The effect sizes (−8 to −12 PANSS points) are modest and clinically meaningful but not clearly superior to existing antipsychotics. Long-term safety, efficacy in treatment-resistant populations, and effects on negative/cognitive symptoms remain uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Xanomeline-trospium offers a new mechanism for symptom control in schizophrenia with a favourable tolerability profile, but its definitive role awaits head-to-head trials and broader real-world data before practice changes can be recommended.

item.title: [9] Treatment Preferences in Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Systematic Review of Discrete Choice Experiment and Best-Worst Scaling Studies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined how children, adolescents, and adults with ADHD, as well as caregivers, value different attributes of ADHD treatments using discrete choice experiments (DCE) and best-worst scaling (BWS) studies. The review synthesised 15 studies to clarify which treatment features matter most to patients and families.
FINDINGS: Across 15 included studies, the most influential treatment attributes were symptom control (highest priority), followed by side-effect severity and social support. Adults with ADHD placed relatively more weight on side-effect tolerance than caregivers of children. Economic cost ranked lower than clinical outcomes and social support. Methodological quality was generally moderate; PREFS scores indicated variable reporting of participant recruitment and setting.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate in size but heterogeneous in methods and populations. The consistent ranking of symptom control and side effects suggests these domains should anchor shared decision-making, while cost appears less decisive. However, the review highlights gaps in longitudinal data, inclusion of behavioural interventions, and culturally diverse samples, limiting generalisability. Small sample sizes and variable study quality temper confidence in precise effect sizes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians can use these preference patterns to guide initial discussions—prioritising efficacy and tolerability—but should remain alert to individual variation and evolving preferences over time. More robust, longitudinal studies are needed before firm practice recommendations can be made.

item.title: [7] Therapeutic Alliance is Linked With Suicidality Trajectories in Psychotherapy for Late-Life Depression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study investigated whether the therapeutic alliance influences suicidality trajectories during brief remote psychotherapy for middle-aged and older adults with major depression, a population with rising suicide rates. It was a randomized trial of remote interventions with repeated assessments of suicidality and alliance.
FINDINGS: At baseline, 53% (n≈32/60) reported suicidality; post-treatment, 45% were in an absent group, 45% improved, and 10% had persistent suicidality. Mixed-effects models showed stable, strong alliance in the absent and improved groups, but worsening alliance in the persistent group.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary due to small sample size, lack of a control arm, and reliance on post-hoc trajectory classification. The association between alliance and suicidality is plausible but may be confounded by unmeasured factors (e.g., symptom severity, adherence). The study cannot establish causality or clinical significance of the alliance effect.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Findings suggest monitoring therapeutic alliance in older adults receiving brief remote psychotherapy for depression, but do not yet justify changing standard care. Larger, controlled studies are needed to determine whether alliance-focused interventions reduce suicidality.

item.title: [7] [Confidential enquiry into maternal suicide: lessons for clinical practice].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This Dutch confidential enquiry used retrospective qualitative case analysis of five maternal suicides (2021–2024) to identify gaps in care for peripartum women with suicidality and to derive practice recommendations.
FINDINGS: Five recurrent themes emerged: under-recognition of non-medical risk factors and suicidality, lack of regional network agreements for perinatal mental health, inadequate safety-planning, inconsistent reporting, and limited peer-support. Documentation gaps and underreporting were noted but not quantified.
INTERPRETATION: The study is a small, retrospective case series with inherent selection and information bias; findings cannot establish causality or generalizable risk. Nevertheless, the recurring themes align with known perinatal suicide risk factors and service-delivery gaps, suggesting plausible targets for quality improvement. The absence of effect sizes or confidence intervals limits assessment of clinical magnitude.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings reinforce the need for systematic suicide risk assessment in pregnancy and postpartum, clear regional referral pathways, and structured safety planning—changes that can be implemented locally while awaiting higher-quality evidence.

item.title: [6] Modeling change in suicidal ideation among transgender adults: a within-person intensive longitudinal test of gender minority stress and resilience theory.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This within-person intensive longitudinal study (ecological momentary assessment) examined how daily minority stressors and resilience factors influence fluctuations in suicidal ideation (SI) among 47 transgender adults with recent SI, testing gender minority stress and resilience theories in real time.
FINDINGS: Interpersonal and intrapersonal minority stressors predicted proximal increases in SI within hours (within-person effects), but between-person resilience factors did not moderate this relationship as theory predicted. The sample included geographic, age, and gender diversity but was predominantly White (87%), limiting generalisability.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides preliminary evidence that momentary minority stressors acutely worsen SI, supporting targeted interventions. However, the lack of moderation by resilience factors challenges existing theory, and the small, non-diverse sample (especially racial minority representation) constrains external validity. The intensive design strengthens causal inference for within-person effects but cannot address broader social determinants.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should assess and mitigate acute minority stressors (e.g., discrimination, internalized stigma) in suicidal trans patients, while noting that resilience-focused interventions may need refinement. Findings underscore the need for larger, more diverse studies to validate these effects across populations.

item.title: [6] How cyberbullying victimization relates to suicide risk: Evidence of feature-based heterogeneity from double machine learning.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examines whether cyberbullying victimization is associated with increased suicide risk, using a large dataset of social media posts analyzed with advanced machine learning methods to adjust for many potential confounders. The population consists of 3,873 individuals identified as cyberbullying victims and 2,603 controls from Weibo (a Chinese social media platform), with suicide risk inferred from language expression.
FINDINGS: Using Double Machine Learning (DML), the study found a statistically significant positive association between cyberbullying victimization and a CSD-derived suicide-related language score (ATE = 0.34, 95% CI [0.20, 0.48]). The effect was heterogeneous: hopelessness was the strongest predictor of increased risk, while hostility and tentative language further elevated risk; conversely, expressions related to cause, autonomy, and money were associated with reduced risk.
INTERPRETATION: This is a preliminary, observational study using social media data and advanced statistical techniques to explore associations. While the DML approach helps control for many confounders, the study design cannot establish causality. The use of language-based suicide risk proxies (rather than clinical diagnoses or validated scales) and the specific population (Weibo users in China) limit generalizability. The effect size, though statistically significant, is modest and based on inferred risk rather than clinical outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest that cyberbullying victimization may be linked to increased suicide-related language expression, particularly in individuals showing hopelessness or hostility. However, due to the study’s limitations, these results should not yet alter clinical practice. Clinicians should remain vigilant for suicide risk in cyberbullying victims, especially those expressing hopelessness, but further research using clinical outcomes and more diverse populations is needed.

item.title: [6] [Empowering families in OCD treatment: a scoping review].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) often leads to significant impairment in social, academic, and family functioning. While cognitive behavioral therapy with exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the most effective treatment, many patients remain symptomatic. This scoping review aimed to map interventions involving family support and provide guidance for families, given the influence of family accommodation and dynamics on treatment outcomes.
FINDINGS: Twenty-three studies were included in this scoping review. All studies involving family interventions reported statistically significant reductions in OCD symptom severity. Common components of these interventions included psychoeducation, reducing family accommodation, supporting exposure exercises, reward systems, supportive/motivational approaches, open communication, emotion regulation, joint problem-solving, improving family interactions and functioning, self-care, and relapse prevention.
INTERPRETATION: As a scoping review, this study provides an exploratory overview rather than definitive evidence of efficacy. The heterogeneity of included studies and lack of detailed implementation descriptions limit strong conclusions. While all studies reported significant symptom reductions, the absence of standardized interventions and control groups makes it difficult to attribute outcomes solely to family involvement. The review highlights the need for more rigorous research to evaluate the specific impact of practical advice and its implementation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence suggests that involving families in OCD treatment may be beneficial, particularly through psychoeducation and reducing accommodation behaviors. However, the lack of standardized protocols means clinicians should use these strategies cautiously, tailoring them to individual family dynamics. More high-quality research is needed before firm recommendations can be made.

item.title: [6] Study Design and Lessons Learned From Using Google Takeout Donations for Suicide Prevention Research: Prospective Cohort Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether Google Search data can predict suicide risk in a prospective, fully remote cohort of U.S. adults with varying suicide risk (current ideation, past-year attempt, lifetime attempt, or no attempt). It aimed to recruit 1000 participants and collect 1 year of follow-up data via biweekly surveys and Google Search history donations via Google Takeout.
FINDINGS: Out of 15,120 initial records, only 485 participants were enrolled and completed the prospective year. Recruitment was hindered by high dropout (63.7% of prescreened participants) and fraudulent behavior (3.2% of records). Among those who attempted to donate Google Search data, 13.6% failed to download it, and 7.7% lacked sufficient data to meet inclusion criteria.
INTERPRETATION: This prospective cohort study highlights major methodological challenges in using Google Search data for suicide prediction research. The high dropout rate, technical difficulties in data acquisition, and fraudulent participation significantly threaten internal validity and generalizability. While the study provides valuable insights into recruitment and data collection barriers, it does not evaluate the predictive accuracy of Google Search algorithms for suicide risk. The findings underscore the need for improved fraud detection, technical support, and collaboration with tech companies to enable meaningful research in this area.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Currently, there is insufficient evidence to support the use of Google Search data for suicide risk prediction in clinical practice. Clinicians should remain cautious about relying on such data until robust, validated methods are established. Future research must address these methodological barriers before any clinical applications can be considered.

item.title: [22] Depression burden and differential treatment effects in PTSD and substance use disorder comorbidity: findings from Project Harmony.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether baseline depression alters treatment response for individuals with co-occurring PTSD and substance use disorders (SUD) across multiple modalities, using harmonised individual patient data (IPD) from 36 RCTs in Project Harmony.
FINDINGS: No individual-level moderation by depression was detected for PTSD, alcohol, or drug use outcomes. However, study-level depression burden moderated treatment effects: in high-depression contexts, trauma-focused psychotherapy showed stronger post-treatment reductions in PTSD and alcohol use but smaller in-treatment gains; integrated trauma-focused therapy had better in-treatment PTSD outcomes; SUD-focused psychotherapy showed attenuated PTSD improvements and mixed alcohol effects.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests that while individual baseline depression does not meaningfully alter treatment response, the overall depression burden within a study population may influence comparative effectiveness across interventions. The use of IPD and advanced statistical methods strengthens internal validity, but reliance on study-level moderators and lack of adjustment for unmeasured confounders limit causal inference. Findings are preliminary and require replication in diverse settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current results do not support tailoring PTSD/SUD treatment based on individual depression severity. However, clinics serving high-depression populations may see differential benefits across modalities, particularly favoring trauma-focused or integrated approaches for long-term outcomes.

item.title: [17] Association of Self-Reported Clinical Behavior With Guideline Adherence in Schizophrenia and Major Depressive Disorder After Guideline Education.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The EGUIDE project is a nationwide Japanese educational program aiming to improve psychiatrists' adherence to clinical guidelines for schizophrenia and major depressive disorder (MDD). This multicenter observational study (n=1897 psychiatrists) examined whether psychiatrists' self-reported clinical behavior (CB) scores after training correlate with objective measures of guideline adherence (GAR) in their patients (n=5328 schizophrenia, n=3538 MDD).
FINDINGS: CB scores showed very weak positive correlations with GAR (schizophrenia: ρ=0.09–0.14; MDD: ρ=0.08–0.11; all p<0.001). Squared coefficients (~0.006–0.020) indicated CB scores explained <2% of the variation in GAR. Associations persisted in sensitivity analyses adjusting for confounders and clustering, but effect sizes remained small.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is observational and cross-sectional, limiting causal inference. The very weak correlations and minimal explained variance suggest CB scores are a poor proxy for actual guideline adherence. Strengths include large sample size and sensitivity analyses, but limitations include unadjusted patient-level correlations and clustering within psychiatrists/institutions. The findings do not support using self-reported CB as a reliable measure of clinical practice.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify relying on post-training self-reported behavior to assess guideline adherence in routine care. Clinicians should continue to use objective quality indicators rather than self-reports for monitoring practice.

item.title: [12] Caring Contacts and Suicidality Among American Indian and Alaska Native Communities: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether culturally adapted "Caring Contacts" (brief, nondemanding messages of care) added to usual care reduced suicidal ideation, attempts, or hospitalizations among 709 American Indian and Alaska Native adults with active suicidality in a 12-month randomized clinical trial across five communities.
FINDINGS: Both groups showed large reductions in suicidal ideation (SIQ-Jr scores from ~42 to ~23) and past-year suicide attempts (from ~48% to ~14% in the intervention vs ~43% to ~16% in controls). No statistically significant between-group differences were found (details on effect sizes or CIs not provided in the abstract).
INTERPRETATION: The trial was well-powered and conducted in a culturally relevant setting, but the lack of between-group differences suggests Caring Contacts did not confer additional benefit over enhanced usual care. The marked improvements in both arms may reflect regression to the mean, therapeutic engagement at baseline, or the effectiveness of existing resources. The study’s external validity is strong for similar Indigenous communities, but generalizability to other populations is uncertain. Funding sources and blinding details are not specified in the abstract.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Caring Contacts cannot be recommended as an adjunctive suicide prevention strategy in this population based on this trial. Further research should clarify the mechanisms driving improvement in both groups and explore other culturally grounded interventions.

item.title: [10] [The association between blood enzyme activity in patients with depression and delusional disorders and their response to psychopharmacotherapy].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether baseline blood enzyme activity in patients with depression and delusional disorders could predict clinical response to psychopharmacotherapy (PFT). It included 54 patients (18–52 years) with diagnoses across schizophrenia spectrum (SSD) and affective spectrum disorders, assessing PANSS and HAM-D before and after treatment.
FINDINGS: In affective disorders (n=21), CPK correlated with reductions in negative PANSS (R=0.47, p=0.02) and post-treatment negative PANSS (R=-0.52, p=0.01); glutamate dehydrogenase correlated with post-treatment positive PANSS (R=-0.48, p=0.01). In SSD (n=34), CPK and GST correlated with reductions in positive PANSS (R=0.38 and R=0.44, p<0.03). Cluster analysis (n=29 and n=26) showed CPK correlated with multiple PANSS outcomes in the larger cluster (R=0.43–0.53, p<0.02), and GST with negative PANSS in the smaller cluster (R=0.46, p=0.02).
INTERPRETATION: This is a small, exploratory observational study without a control group or validation cohort. Correlations are statistically significant but weak to moderate, and causality cannot be inferred. The lack of adjustment for multiple comparisons and potential confounders (e.g., medication type, dose, duration) limits internal validity. External validity is constrained by the heterogeneous sample and absence of replication. Findings are preliminary and should not guide clinical practice.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No change in practice is warranted based on these results. Future research should validate biomarkers in larger, controlled cohorts with standardized treatment protocols.

item.title: [10] [Effectiveness of biofeedback based on respiratory parameters in the treatment of anxiety and depressive disorders].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review evaluated whether biofeedback (BF) based on respiratory parameters reduces symptoms in patients with clinically confirmed anxiety or depressive disorders, focusing on panic disorder (PD) given the available evidence. Six studies (N=1596) were included: three RCTs, two observational studies, and one case series.
FINDINGS: Across all studies, intra-group effect size for PD severity (PDSS) in BF groups was Hedges' g=1.34 (95% CI 1.27–1.41; p<0.001; I²=88%). In two RCTs comparing BF to waiting list, intergroup effect size was g=1.53 (95% CI 0.23–2.83; p=0.022; I²=87%). Two RCTs also showed greater reduction in depressive symptoms (BDI) with BF vs waiting list (g=1.64; 95% CI 0.87–2.41; p<0.001; I²=64%). No serious adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests large short-term improvements in PD and depressive symptoms with respiratory BF, but confidence in these findings is low due to high heterogeneity, small number of RCTs, lack of active comparators, and high risk of bias. The absence of long-term follow-up and potential publication bias further limit reliability. The large effect sizes may reflect placebo or regression to the mean rather than true efficacy.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Respiratory biofeedback may be considered as an adjunctive option for PD, but current evidence is insufficient to recommend it as a first-line treatment. Clinicians should monitor for symptom change and remain cautious about overinterpreting preliminary data. Further high-quality RCTs with active controls and long-term follow-up are needed.

item.title: [7] Quality of media reporting of suicidal behaviour in India.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined the quality of media reporting on suicidal behaviour in India, a country with high suicide rates, against WHO and Press Council of India (PCI) guidelines. It used a content analysis of 117 newspaper articles published in January 2023.
FINDINGS: All 117 articles contained at least one harmful element per WHO guidelines. Names (79.5%), occupation (49.6%), and method (82.9%) were frequently disclosed. A single cause was cited in 58.1% of cases, with negative life events mentioned in 63.2%. Only 28.2% included any helpful information, and PCI 2022 guidelines were violated across all domains.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is robust in documenting widespread non-adherence to established media guidelines, but it is observational and descriptive, limiting causal inference. The study highlights a clear gap between recommended and actual practice, though it does not assess the impact of reporting on suicide rates. The sample is limited to six newspapers over one month, which may not reflect broader trends.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be aware that sensational or detailed media reporting of suicide may contribute to contagion effects. Advocacy for adherence to WHO/Press Council guidelines remains important, but the study does not quantify the clinical impact of such reporting.

item.title: [6] Learning from deaths to improve lives: why England still needs a national LeDeR programme.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This commentary discusses the rationale for England’s Learning from Deaths (LeDeR) programme, a national mortality review system for people with intellectual disabilities and autistic people, and warns against its discontinuation due to risks of overlooking preventable deaths and inequities in healthcare.
FINDINGS: The LeDeR programme is described as the world’s only national system for reviewing deaths in this population. The authors argue that abandoning national surveillance would reduce visibility of preventable deaths, potentially worsening healthcare inequities.
INTERPRETATION: This is a commentary rather than empirical research, so it lacks quantitative data, effect sizes, or statistical analysis. The strength of the argument depends on the plausibility of the risks described rather than measured outcomes. The external validity is limited to the UK context, and the generalisability to other healthcare systems is uncertain. The authors’ conclusion is framed as a warning rather than evidence-based.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This piece highlights the importance of systematic mortality review in vulnerable populations but does not provide actionable clinical data. It serves as a call to maintain or improve such programmes rather than a basis for changing practice.

item.title: [6] Medicating inhibitory control? Treatment with serotonergic antidepressants predicts stop-N200 amplitudes in major depressive disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This observational study examined whether serotonergic antidepressants, sex, or comorbid anxiety disorders (COM) influence neural indices of inhibitory control in major depressive disorder (MDD) using EEG during a stop-signal task. The Tulsa 1000 cohort included healthy controls (HCs), MDD, and COM participants.
FINDINGS: HCs showed larger stop-P300 amplitudes than MDD/COM (η² = 0.068). Females had smaller stop-N200 amplitudes than males (η² = 0.027). Among MDD/COM, serotonergic antidepressant use was associated with less negative N200 amplitudes (LME, B = 1.95; η² = 0.044; ATE, B = 2.47).
INTERPRETATION: The study’s cross-sectional design limits causal inference; antidepressant exposure was not randomized, and unmeasured confounders (e.g., symptom severity, illness duration) may bias results. The effect sizes (η² ≤ 0.068) are small, suggesting limited clinical relevance despite statistical significance. The use of propensity matching strengthens internal validity but does not eliminate residual confounding.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support changing prescribing practices based on these neural indices. Further longitudinal or interventional studies are needed to determine whether serotonergic antidepressants causally alter inhibitory control or if observed differences reflect pre-existing traits.

item.title: [6] Serum selenium, iron and rubidium are altered in treatment-resistant schizophrenia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This exploratory cohort study examined serum levels of selenium, iron, rubidium, and related inflammatory and antioxidant markers in people with treatment-resistant schizophrenia (TRS) compared to controls, aiming to clarify metabolic disturbances that may contribute to oxidative stress and inflammation in schizophrenia.
FINDINGS: The TRS cohort (n=~100) showed significantly lower serum selenium (effect size not reported), lower selenoprotein-P1 and GPX3, and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines and hepcidin compared to controls (n=~100). Serum iron was reduced and rubidium elevated in TRS. These differences remained after adjusting for age and clozapine levels, with discrimination between groups reported but no explicit AUC or sensitivity/specificity values provided.
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests systemic oxidative and inflammatory dysregulation in TRS, but as a non-randomized, non-blinded cohort, causal inference is limited. The lack of effect sizes and diagnostic performance metrics makes it unclear how clinically useful these biomarkers would be. Funding sources and potential conflicts are not stated, which is a limitation in interpreting objectivity. Further research linking peripheral and central measures is needed before any clinical application.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings do not yet support changes in routine practice. They highlight potential biological pathways in TRS that may guide future research into novel treatments targeting oxidative stress or inflammation, but biomarkers for diagnosis or treatment selection remain investigational.

item.title: [6] Dynamic epigenetic changes during antidepressant pharmacotherapy in major depressive disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study investigated whether dynamic changes in DNA methylation during antidepressant treatment in major depressive disorder (MDD) could serve as biomarkers for treatment response. This longitudinal epigenome-wide association study (EWAS) followed 162 MDD patients (81 responders, 81 non-responders) and 48 healthy controls over eight weeks of standardized antidepressant therapy to identify methylation patterns linked to clinical outcomes.
FINDINGS: Baseline methylation levels in two and six differentially methylated regions (DMRs) were associated with depressive symptom severity at day 28 and day 56, respectively (e.g., genes *TNRC6C*, *CAT*). No single differentially methylated position (DMP) reached significance. Longitudinal analyses identified one DMP (*YLMP1*) linked to symptom improvement and three DMRs (*GPR126*, *PM20D1*) showing time-dependent methylation changes. Combined patient-control analyses revealed additional DMPs and DMRs tied to diagnosis and temporal effects.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides preliminary longitudinal evidence of coordinated methylation changes during antidepressant treatment, implicating genes involved in neuroplasticity and inflammation. However, the findings are exploratory, with small effect sizes and no single DMP reaching genome-wide significance. The lack of replication and functional validation limits clinical applicability. The design is robust for an EWAS (longitudinal sampling, standardized treatment), but external validity is constrained by the specific cohort and short follow-up.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These results do not yet justify changes in practice but suggest potential epigenetic biomarkers for antidepressant response. Future studies must validate these findings and clarify their biological relevance before considering clinical use.

item.title: [6] The molecular and neurochemical basis of altered intrinsic neural timescales in major depressive disorder: a multimodal imaging-transcriptomic investigation of esketamine and sertraline treatment.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This multimodal neuroimaging-transcriptomic study examined how intrinsic neural timescales (INT)—a measure of local brain information integration—change in major depressive disorder (MDD) and after treatment with esketamine and sertraline. It included 41 MDD patients and 57 healthy controls, using resting-state fMRI, spatial transcriptomics, and PET receptor mapping to link neural dynamics to molecular and neurochemical features.
FINDINGS: At baseline, MDD patients showed elevated INT in the bilateral precuneus and reduced INT in the default mode network (DMN) versus controls. After treatment, INT increased in the left occipital midline and left calcarine cortex, and in the cerebellar network (CN). Spatial correlation with gene expression suggested associations with immune response, hormonal regulation, and glutamatergic synapses, while INT changes correlated with 5-HT1b and NAT receptor density. However, the primary spatial correlation did not reach conventional significance (r = 0.484, p = 0.068).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides preliminary evidence that MDD involves altered INT in higher-order cortical and DMN regions, with partial normalization after treatment. The exploratory transcriptomic and receptor mapping findings are hypothesis-generating and should be interpreted cautiously due to the lack of statistical significance in the main spatial correlation. The sample size is modest, and the multimodal approach increases complexity without resolving causal pathways.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings do not yet translate into clinical practice but suggest potential biomarkers for treatment response and targets for novel interventions. Further validation in larger, controlled studies is needed before any bedside application.

item.title: [6] Real-World Status of Augmentation Therapy With Atypical Antipsychotics in Major Depressive Disorder: A Claims Database Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective cohort study from Japan used a large claims database to describe real-world treatment patterns, especially atypical antipsychotic (AAP) augmentation, in adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) who started antidepressant monotherapy as first-line therapy (LOT1) between 2013 and 2020.
FINDINGS: Of 50 355 patients initiating antidepressant monotherapy, 7.6 % (n = 3 811) later received AAP augmentation after a mean of 1.4 prior lines of therapy and 270 days. Within 180 days after starting augmentation, 37.9 % switched to another regimen, while 46.4 % persisted on AAP augmentation for ≥ 180 days. Overall, 14.6 % of LOT1 patients went on to ≥ 3 lines of therapy, most commonly repeating SSRI monotherapy.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is observational and subject to coding errors, channelling bias, and lack of clinical outcomes (e.g., symptom change). Persistence data suggest that about half of patients continue augmentation for at least six months, but the long interval (≈ 9 months) from monotherapy initiation to augmentation raises questions about optimal timing. No causal inferences about efficacy can be drawn.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These real-world patterns may guide expectations about how often and when clinicians in Japan add AAPs, but they do not establish whether earlier or later augmentation improves outcomes; decisions should still be guided by individual risk–benefit assessment and guideline recommendations.

item.title: [12] INTENSIFY-a randomized, controlled trial to investigate the effect of an early intensified pharmacological treatment for major psychiatric disorders after treatment failure in the current episode: a study protocol.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The INTENSIFY trial is a planned set of three international, multicentre, open-label randomized controlled trials (RCTs) designed to test whether switching adults (≥18 years) with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, major depressive disorder, or bipolar depression to a third-line pharmacological treatment immediately after failure of first-line therapy improves symptom reduction within 6 weeks compared with continuing second-line treatment as usual.
FINDINGS: The study plans to randomize 1254 participants across at least 16 sites. The primary outcome is change in symptom severity after 6 weeks, to be analyzed using ANCOVA. Secondary outcomes include cognitive function, quality of life, functional measures, digital mental health markers, side effects, and concomitant medication. The trial is registered under multiple identifiers (NCT05603104, NCT05958875, NCT05973786, NCT05973851, ACTRN12625000327482, ACTRN12625000328471, ACTRN12625000329460).
INTERPRETATION: This is a well-powered, multi-country RCT protocol with clearly defined primary and secondary endpoints. Its open-label design and 6-week duration limit the ability to draw long-term conclusions about safety, tolerability, and sustained efficacy. The lack of blinding and potential cross-trial heterogeneity across diagnostic groups (schizophrenia, bipolar depression, major depression) may introduce bias and complicate interpretation. Results will be relevant mainly if they demonstrate clinically meaningful differences in symptom reduction and functional outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: If positive, these findings could support earlier use of third-line treatments in treatment-resistant presentations, potentially prompting updates to treatment guidelines. Until results are published, clinicians should continue to follow existing stepwise treatment algorithms and monitor for adverse effects when intensifying pharmacotherapy.

item.title: [11] Dorsomedial prefrontal cortex repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation combined with antidepressants in major depressive disorder: a randomized, double-blind, single-center, sham-controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This single-center, double-blind, sham-controlled RCT (n=60) tested whether adding dorsomedial prefrontal cortex rTMS (DMPFC-rTMS) or conventional high-frequency left-prefrontal rTMS (HF-rTMS) to newly started SSRIs improves acute outcomes in adults with a current major depressive episode.
FINDINGS: After 20 sessions, MADRS reductions were −14.3 (95 % CI −18.3 to −10.3) with DMPFC-rTMS, −8.2 (−11.7 to −4.7) with HF-rTMS, and −12.6 (−16.1 to −9.0) with sham. Pairwise comparisons showed no statistically significant differences (all p > 0.05). Response/remission rates were 35 %/20 % (DMPFC), 30 %/15 % (HF), and 55 %/45 % (sham); dropout rates were 45 %, 25 %, and 25 %. No serious adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The trial is underpowered (n≈60) and shows a large sham response, making it unlikely to detect small incremental effects of rTMS on top of SSRI initiation. The high attrition in the DMPFC arm further limits interpretability. Until replicated in larger, adequately powered studies with optimized parameters, these results should be considered exploratory and not practice-changing.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine use of DMPFC-rTMS or HF-rTMS as an add-on to newly initiated SSRIs for acute MDD; clinicians should continue to follow established rTMS indications and protocols.

item.title: [10] Peripheral molecular signatures of major depressive disorder: a systematic review of blood-derived biomarkers for diagnosis, stratification, and treatment response.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This PRISMA-compliant systematic review (PROSPERO-registered) evaluated blood-derived molecular biomarkers for diagnosing major depressive disorder (MDD), stratifying subtypes, or predicting treatment response, given the current symptom-based approach and biological heterogeneity of MDD.
FINDINGS: From 9,354 records, 25 eligible studies (24 independent datasets) were identified, covering transcriptomics, DNA methylation, immune-inflammatory markers, and multi-omics. Recurrent pathway-level signals included immune-inflammatory and interferon pathways, NF-κB signaling, mitochondrial metabolism, epigenetic regulation, and non-coding RNA. Multi-marker panels showed potential for diagnosis or predicting treatment response but were largely exploratory, cohort-specific, or internally validated. Modified GRADE certainty was rated low to very low across domains.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous, with no single biomarker or panel ready for clinical use. Pathway-level convergence suggests biological plausibility but lacks external validation or standardized platforms. Methodological limitations (small samples, cohort-specific findings, lack of prospective validation) and low GRADE certainty mean results should be interpreted cautiously. The review highlights the need for larger, harmonized, multi-center studies with rigorous validation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No blood-derived biomarker is currently recommended for routine diagnosis, stratification, or treatment selection in MDD. These findings support continued research but do not change current clinical practice. Clinicians should await validated, externally validated tools before considering biomarker-guided care.

item.title: [9] State-dependent effects of rTMS on cognitive function in bipolar II disorder: A randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether pairing 10-Hz rTMS to the left inferior parietal lobule with a complex cognitive task enhances working-memory outcomes versus a simple task or sham stimulation in 96 euthymic adults with bipolar II disorder and subjective cognitive complaints, using a 2×2 factorial RCT design.
FINDINGS: Eighty-three of 96 participants completed the trial. No stimulation-by-task interaction survived FDR correction. Nominal interactions for angular error (overall and at set size 2) did not reach corrected significance. Within-group improvements were most consistent in the active rTMS + simple task arm, but no factorial condition showed superiority. PDQ scores improved across all groups without significant between-group differences. Exploratory fMRI analyses showed divergent connectivity changes across conditions.
INTERPRETATION: The trial provides moderate-quality evidence against a robust synergistic effect of concurrent complex cognitive engagement on rTMS-related working-memory gains in euthymic bipolar II disorder. Strengths include the randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled factorial design and neuronavigated targeting. Limitations include the exploratory nature, absence of correction for neuroimaging outcomes, and lack of an active cognitive-task-only arm to isolate task effects. The observed within-group improvements are likely attributable to practice or nonspecific factors rather than a true stimulation-task interaction.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data do not support adding complex cognitive tasks to rTMS protocols for working-memory enhancement in euthymic bipolar II disorder. Future studies should optimize stimulation parameters and cognitive-load timing before testing in routine care.

item.title: [8] Transcriptional profiling of antidepressant ketamine and electroconvulsive therapy treatment.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether peripheral blood gene expression could serve as a biomarker for treatment response in treatment-resistant depression (TRD) patients undergoing electroconvulsive therapy (ECT, N=37) or ketamine infusions (N=60), compared to non-depressed controls (N=35). The goal was to identify transcriptional changes associated with diagnosis, treatment, and clinical response/remission.
FINDINGS: No significant longitudinal transcriptional changes were detected for either treatment at the single-gene or network level (FDR-corrected or |logFC| >0.05). In the ketamine group, baseline comparisons between remitters and non-remitters showed enrichment for immune-related functions, with one gene (IGKV1-9) significantly differentially expressed (p = 2.5E-05, logFC = -0.51). In the ECT group, six co-regulated gene modules differed at baseline between patients and controls, with significant time-diagnosis interaction effects in gene networks.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s internal validity is strengthened by its longitudinal design, multiple time points, and rigorous statistical correction (FDR, WGCNA). However, the lack of detectable longitudinal changes despite robust clinical improvements suggests peripheral blood RNA-seq may not capture mechanistic antidepressant effects. The small effect size (logFC = -0.51) and single significant gene in ketamine remitters limit clinical utility. Findings are preliminary, and larger samples are needed to validate predictive biomarkers.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support peripheral blood gene expression as a biomarker for monitoring ECT or ketamine response in TRD. Baseline differences may hint at predictive signatures, but these are not yet actionable for clinical decision-making. Further research is required before considering such testing in routine care.

item.title: [12] Oral Esketamine Maintenance Treatment for Treatment-Resistant Depression: Clinical Outcomes During an Off-Label Treatment Program.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This observational cohort study examined whether long-term at-home oral esketamine maintenance (max 3.0 mg/kg twice weekly) sustains antidepressant effects in adults with severe treatment-resistant unipolar depression after an initial 6-week clinic-based induction. The clinical question is whether maintenance dosing can preserve symptom control and safety over a median 20.8 months.
FINDINGS: Among 93 patients entering maintenance, the mean HDRS17 change from baseline to last observation was 0.825 points (95% CI −0.759 to 2.410, p = 0.302). Of 26 initial responders (≥50% HDRS17 reduction), 23.1% sustained response during maintenance; of 40 meeting MCID (≥27.1% reduction), 60.0% sustained MCID. Eleven patients (11.8%) successfully tapered off; 12 (12.9%) discontinued due to adverse events.
INTERPRETATION: The lack of significant change in HDRS17 scores suggests that symptom severity remained stable rather than improving during maintenance, but the single-arm design and absence of a comparator preclude causal inference. The high discontinuation rate due to adverse events (12.9%) and the modest sustained-response rate among initial responders (23.1%) temper enthusiasm. Safety monitoring remains essential given unknown long-term risks. The study’s external validity is limited by selection of TRD patients able to tolerate induction and by the absence of randomization or blinding.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Oral esketamine maintenance may help some patients with TRD maintain symptom stability, but the evidence is observational and does not demonstrate superiority over continued standard care. Clinicians should weigh uncertain long-term safety, adverse-event risk, and modest sustained-response rates when considering at-home maintenance.
